title: Amos 4:10 (#1)
content:
דֶּ֨בֶר֙ בְּ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ מִצְרַ֔יִם

"a plague in the way of Egypt"

Yahweh is using a plague in the way of Egypt to mean a plague like the ones that he sent on the Egyptians. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a plague like the ones I sent on the Egyptians]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 4:10 (#2)
content:
הָרַ֤גְתִּי בַ⁠חֶ֨רֶב֙ בַּח֣וּרֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"I killed your young men with the sword"

Here, the sword represents “warfare.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I allowed your enemies to kill your young men in warfare]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 4:10 (#3)
content:
בְּאֹ֤שׁ מַחֲנֵי⁠כֶם֙

"the stench of your camp"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that Yahweh caused the stench of the corpses of those killed to rise from where the Israelites were camped. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the stench of the corpses in your camp]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 4:11 (#1)
content:
הָפַ֣כְתִּי בָ⁠כֶ֗ם כְּ⁠מַהְפֵּכַ֤ת אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת־סְדֹ֣ם וְ⁠אֶת־עֲמֹרָ֔ה

"I overthrew among you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah"

The point of this comparison is that just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah so completely that nothing was left of them, so the destruction that Yahweh brought on the Israelites was devastating. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I brought devastating destruction among you, just as God so completely destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah that nothing was left of them]

See: Simile

title: Amos 4:11 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠תִּהְי֕וּ כְּ⁠א֖וּד מֻצָּ֣ל מִ⁠שְׂרֵפָ֑ה

"and you were like a firebrand snatched from a burning"

The point of this comparison is that just as a firebrand snatched from a burning is charred and barely saved, so the Israelites who survived were rescued only barely and at great cost. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and some of you barely survived, as though you had been pulled out of a fire at the last moment]

See: Simile

title: Amos 4:11 (#3)
content:
כְּ⁠א֖וּד מֻצָּ֣ל

"like a firebrand snatched"

The expression snatched from a burning is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like a firebrand that someone snatched]

See: Active or Passive

title: Amos 4:12 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠כֵ֕ן כֹּ֥ה אֶעֱשֶׂה־לְּ⁠ךָ֖ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"Therefore, thus I will do to you, Israel"

The word translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because you would not return to me, this is what I will do to you, Israel]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Amos 4:12 (#2)
content:
לְּ⁠ךָ֖ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"to you, Israel"

Israel represents the people of Israel. Alternate translation: [to you Israelites]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 4:12 (#3)
content:
עֵ֚קֶב כִּֽי־זֹ֣את אֶֽעֱשֶׂה־לָּ֔⁠ךְ הִכּ֥וֹן לִ⁠קְרַאת־אֱלֹהֶ֖י⁠ךָ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"for the reason that I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel"

The words translated as for the reason that indicate that what follows is a reason for the command that comes after it. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason. Alternate translation: [and since I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Amos 4:12 (#4)
content:
הִכּ֥וֹן לִ⁠קְרַאת־אֱלֹהֶ֖י⁠ךָ

"prepare to meet your God"

The word translated as prepare is an imperative, but it communicates a solemn warning rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a warning. Alternate translation: [be prepared to meet your God]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Amos 4:13 (#1)
content:
כִּ֡י הִנֵּה֩

"For behold"

The word translated as For connects this description of Yahweh to what he has just said, that they should “prepare to meet” their God, and the word behold calls attention to what follows. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [In fact, you will need to prepare to meet your God by carefully considering that he is]

See: Connecting Words and Phrases

title: Amos 4:13 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מַגִּ֤יד לְ⁠אָדָם֙ מַה־שֵּׂח֔⁠וֹ

"and declaring to man what {is} his thought"

This could mean: (1) God declares to people their own inward thoughts and motivations, as in the UST. (2) God reveals to people what he, God, is thinking. Alternate translation: [and declaring to man God’s own plans]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 4:13 (#3)
content:
מַה־שֵּׂח֔⁠וֹ

"what {is} his thought"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of thought, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he is thinking]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 4:13 (#4)
content:
עֹשֵׂ֥ה שַׁ֨חַר֙ עֵיפָ֔ה

"making dawn darkness"

This could mean: (1) God makes everything from morning light to the darkness of night. Alternate translation: [making all times of light and darkness] or (2) God causes morning to become night. Alternate translation: [making dawn into darkness]

See: Merism

title: Amos 4:13 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠דֹרֵ֖ךְ עַל־בָּ֣מֳתֵי אָ֑רֶץ

"and treading on the high places of the earth"

Amos is speaking of Yahweh ruling over the whole earth as if he were treading on the high places of the earth. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and ruling over the whole earth]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 4:13 (#6)
content:
אֱלֹהֵֽי־צְבָא֖וֹת

"God of Armies"

Amos is using this possessive form to mean the God who commands the armies of heaven. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who commands the armies of heaven]

See: Possession

title: Amos 4:13 (#7)
content:
שְׁמֽ⁠וֹ

"is} his name"

Amos is using the term name to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to the Yahweh’s reputation. Alternate translation: [this is who he is]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos - Chapter 5 Introduction
content:
Amos 5 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

  1. Yahweh mourns Israel’s coming downfall (1–3)
  2. Yahweh calls Israel to seek him and reject injustice (4–17)
  3. Yahweh warns of the coming day of Yahweh (18–20)
  4. Yahweh rejects empty worship and demands justice (21–27)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The gate

Elders decided legal cases at the city gate, so the wrongs in 5:10 and 5:12 are abuses of the courts.

The day of Yahweh

Israel expected this “day of Yahweh” to bring victory, but it will bring judgment.

title: Amos 5:1 (#1)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֗ה

"this word"

Here, this word represents “the message that Yahweh is giving through Amos.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [this message]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:1 (#2)
content:
אָנֹכִ֜י נֹשֵׂ֧א עֲלֵי⁠כֶ֛ם

"I am lifting up over you"

Amos is speaking as if the song of mourning that he is singing were a heavy object that he was lifting up over the people of Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am singing about you]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:1 (#3)
content:
קִינָ֖ה

"a lamentation"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of lamentation, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a mournful song]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:1 (#4)
content:
בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"house of Israel"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Israel means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [all you Israelites]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:2 (#1)
content:
נִטְּשָׁ֥ה עַל־אַדְמָתָ֖⁠הּ

"She is forsaken on her land"

The expression is forsaken is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Her enemies have left her lying on her land]

See: Active or Passive

title: Amos 5:2 (#2)
content:
נָֽפְלָה֙ לֹֽא־תוֹסִ֣יף ק֔וּם בְּתוּלַ֖ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"She has fallen; she will not repeat to rise, the virgin Israel"

Amos is speaking of the nation of Israel being vulnerable as if it were a young virgin woman who has fallen down and who will never rise again. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The nation of Israel has been defeated; she will never regain her power]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:2 (#3)
content:
נָֽפְלָה֙

"She has fallen"

The pronoun She refers to the nation of Israel, whom Amos names as the virgin Israel later in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The nation of Israel has fallen]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 5:2 (#4)
content:
אֵ֥ין מְקִימָֽ⁠הּ

"there is no one raising her up"

Here Amos is speaking of there being no one to help Israel as if it were a woman who had physically “fallen” and no one is raising her up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly or use a comparable expression. Alternate translation: [there is no one to help her recover]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:3 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠עִ֛יר הַ⁠יֹּצֵ֥את אֶ֖לֶף

"The city going out a thousand"

Here, The city represents “the fighting men who march out from the city.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [A thousand fighting men marching out from a city]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:3 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠יֹּצֵ֥את אֶ֖לֶף תַּשְׁאִ֣יר מֵאָ֑ה

"going out a thousand will leave a hundred remaining"

Here, a thousand and a hundred represent groups of soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled in the UST.

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:3 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"for the house of Israel"

See how you translated these same phrases in 5:1.

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:3 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"for the house of Israel"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to defend the people of Israel]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 5:4 (#1)
content:
דִּרְשׁ֖וּ⁠נִי וִֽ⁠חְיֽוּ

"Seek me and live"

Yahweh is speaking as if the people could Seek him, as though he were something lost that they could look for and find. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Devote yourselves to me and live]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:4 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠בֵ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"to the house of Israel"

See how you translated the same phrase “house of Israel” in 5:1.

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:4 (#3)
content:
דִּרְשׁ֖וּ⁠נִי וִֽ⁠חְיֽוּ

"Seek me and live"

The word translated as Seek is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [If you seek me, then you will live]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

title: Amos 5:5 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אַֽל־תִּדְרְשׁוּ֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל וְ⁠הַ⁠גִּלְגָּל֙ לֹ֣א תָבֹ֔אוּ וּ⁠בְאֵ֥ר שֶׁ֖בַע לֹ֣א תַעֲבֹ֑רוּ כִּ֤י הַ⁠גִּלְגָּל֙ גָּלֹ֣ה יִגְלֶ֔ה וּ⁠בֵֽית־אֵ֖ל יִהְיֶ֥ה לְ⁠אָֽוֶן

"and do not seek Bethel, and do not go to Gilgal, and do not cross over to Beersheba; for Gilgal, going into exile, will go into exile, and Bethel will become iniquity"

Yahweh uses the word and here to indicate a contrast between seeking him and seeking the shrines at Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but do not seek Bethel; instead of going to Gilgal or crossing over to Beersheba, remember that Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will become iniquity.]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Amos 5:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אַֽל־תִּדְרְשׁוּ֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל

"and do not seek Bethel"

Yahweh is speaking of devoting themselves and worshiping at Bethel as if the people could seek and find something that had been lost. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and do not devote yourselves to worshiping at Bethel]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:5 (#3)
content:
בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל

"Bethel"

Here, Bethel represents “the shrine at Bethel where the people worshiped.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the shrine at Bethel]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:5 (#4)
content:
הַ⁠גִּלְגָּל֙ גָּלֹ֣ה יִגְלֶ֔ה

"Gilgal, going into exile, will go into exile"

The words translated as going into exile, will go into exile sound like the name of the town, Gilgal. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Amos 5:5 (#5)
content:
גָּלֹ֣ה יִגְלֶ֔ה

"going into exile, will go into exile"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb go into exile in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [for Gilgal will certainly go into exile]

See: Reduplication

title: Amos 5:5 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠בֵֽית־אֵ֖ל יִהְיֶ֥ה לְ⁠אָֽוֶן

"and Bethel will become iniquity"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of iniquity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and Bethel will become an evil place]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:5 (#7)
content:
וּ⁠בֵֽית־אֵ֖ל יִהְיֶ֥ה לְ⁠אָֽוֶן

"and Bethel will become iniquity"

Here, Bethel represents “the worship that the people offer at Bethel.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the worship at Bethel will become iniquity]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:6 (#1)
content:
דִּרְשׁ֥וּ אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה וִֽ⁠חְי֑וּ

"Seek Yahweh and live"

Amos is speaking as if the people could Seek Yahweh, as though he were something lost that they could look for and find. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Devote yourselves to Yahweh and live]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:6 (#2)
content:
פֶּן־יִצְלַ֤ח

"lest he break out"

Amos is using the word translated as lest to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the people of Israel an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [otherwise, he will break out]

See: Connect — Goal (Purpose) Relationship

title: Amos 5:6 (#3)
content:
פֶּן־יִצְלַ֤ח כָּ⁠אֵשׁ֙ בֵּ֣ית יוֹסֵ֔ף

"lest he break out like fire {in} the house of Joseph"

The point of this comparison is that just as fire spreads swiftly and destroys everything in its path, so Yahweh’s judgment will come swiftly and destroy the descendants of Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [lest he break out against the house of Joseph like a fire that spreads swiftly and destroys everything in its path]

See: Simile

title: Amos 5:6 (#4)
content:
בֵּ֣ית יוֹסֵ֔ף

"in} the house of Joseph"

Here the term house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Joseph means all the people descended from the patriarch Joseph. By this time, those descendants had become the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. Alternate translation: [among the descendants of Joseph] or [among the people of the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:6 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אָכְלָ֥ה וְ⁠אֵין־מְכַבֶּ֖ה לְ⁠בֵֽית־אֵֽל

"and it consumes, and there is no extinguisher for Bethel"

is speaking as if Yahweh’s judgment against them were a fire that consumes them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his judgment will destroy Bethel, and no one will be able to stop it]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:6 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠אָכְלָ֥ה

"and it consumes"

The pronoun it refers to the fire that Yahweh will send. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the fire consumes]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 5:7 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠הֹפְכִ֥ים לְ⁠לַעֲנָ֖ה מִשְׁפָּ֑ט

"the {ones} turning justice into wormwood"

Amos is speaking to those who have distorted justice as if justice were something that they could change into wormwood, a poisonous plant with a very bitter taste. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who have distorted justice for people]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:7 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠הֹפְכִ֥ים לְ⁠לַעֲנָ֖ה מִשְׁפָּ֑ט

"the {ones} turning justice into wormwood"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of justice, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones turning what is just into something bitter]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:7 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠צְדָקָ֖ה לָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הִנִּֽיחוּ

"and they cast righteousness to the ground"

Amos is speaking of rejecting righteousness as if righteousness were an object that these people could cast down to the ground and leave there. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they completely reject righteousness]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:7 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠צְדָקָ֖ה לָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הִנִּֽיחוּ

"and they cast righteousness to the ground"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of righteousness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they cast what is right to the ground]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:8 (#1)
content:
עֹשֵׂ֨ה כִימָ֜ה וּ⁠כְסִ֗יל וְ⁠הֹפֵ֤ךְ לַ⁠בֹּ֨קֶר֙ צַלְמָ֔וֶת וְ⁠י֖וֹם לַ֣יְלָה הֶחְשִׁ֑יךְ הַ⁠קּוֹרֵ֣א לְ⁠מֵֽי־הַ⁠יָּ֗ם וַֽ⁠יִּשְׁפְּכֵ֛⁠ם עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ יְהוָ֥ה שְׁמֽ⁠וֹ

"The maker of the Pleiades and Orion, turning deep darkness into morning; he darkens day into night; calling for the waters of the sea, he pours them out on the face of the earth— Yahweh is his name"

Amos describes Yahweh as the one with power over all he created by a series of phrases and only names him at the end of the verse. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about who Yahweh is before the information about what he does. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is the maker of the Pleiades and Orion, turning deep darkness into morning; he darkens day into night; calling for the waters of the sea, he pours them out on the face of the earth.]

See: Information Structure

title: Amos 5:8 (#2)
content:
כִימָ֜ה וּ⁠כְסִ֗יל

"the Pleiades and Orion"

The terms Pleiades and Orion are the names of groups of stars in the night sky. If your readers would not be familiar with what these are, you could use the names of star groups that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the groups of stars in the sky]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Amos 5:8 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הֹפֵ֤ךְ לַ⁠בֹּ֨קֶר֙ צַלְמָ֔וֶת וְ⁠י֖וֹם לַ֣יְלָה הֶחְשִׁ֑יךְ

"turning deep darkness into morning; he darkens day into night"

Amos is referring to all of time by naming the two major components, morning and night. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [governing the passing of all time, from morning until night]

See: Merism

title: Amos 5:8 (#4)
content:
עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ

"on the face of the earth"

Amos is using the face of the earth as a common expression of the culture to mean “the surface of the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everywhere on the earth]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 5:8 (#5)
content:
יְהוָ֥ה שְׁמֽ⁠וֹ

"Yahweh is his name"

Amos is using the term name to represent who the Yahweh is or to refer to the Yahweh’s reputation. Alternate translation: [This is Yahweh himself]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:9 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠מַּבְלִ֥יג שֹׁ֖ד עַל־עָ֑ז

"the one making destruction flash against the strong"

Amos is speaking destroying the strong as if destruction were lightning that Yahweh could make flash suddenly against strong people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one bringing sudden ruin upon the strong]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:9 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠מַּבְלִ֥יג שֹׁ֖ד עַל־עָ֑ז וְ⁠שֹׁ֖ד עַל & יָבֽוֹא

"the one making destruction flash against the strong, and destruction comes against"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of destruction, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one suddenly destroying the strong, and he destroys]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:9 (#3)
content:
עַל־עָ֑ז

"against the strong"

Amos is using the adjective strong as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [against those who are strong]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Amos 5:10 (#1)
content:
שָׂנְא֥וּ בַ⁠שַּׁ֖עַר מוֹכִ֑יחַ

"They hate the reprover in the gate"

The pronoun They refers to the strong referred to in the previous verse, or those who are influential people of Israel whom Amos is condemning. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Those of you who are strong hate the reprover in the gate]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 5:10 (#2)
content:
בַ⁠שַּׁ֖עַר מוֹכִ֑יחַ

"the reprover in the gate"

Here, the gate represents “the place where the leaders of a city decided legal cases.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the reprover at the place of judgment]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:11 (#1)
content:
יַ֣עַן בּוֹשַׁסְ⁠כֶ֞ם עַל־דָּ֗ל

"because of your trampling on the poor"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of trampling, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you trample on the poor]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:11 (#2)
content:
כַּרְמֵי־חֶ֣מֶד

"vineyards of desire"

The implication is that these are vineyards that are pleasant and desirable. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [delightful vineyards]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 5:11 (#3)
content:
בּוֹשַׁסְ⁠כֶ֞ם עַל־דָּ֗ל

"of your trampling on the poor"

Amos is speaking those who are mistreating poor people as if these people were trampling on the poor beneath their feet. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are mistreating the poor]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:11 (#4)
content:
דָּ֗ל

"the poor"

Amos is using the adjective poor as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are poor]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Amos 5:12 (#1)
content:
רַבִּ֣ים פִּשְׁעֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וַ⁠עֲצֻמִ֖ים חַטֹּֽאתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"your transgressions {are} many, and your sins {are} mighty"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of transgressions and sins, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [that you have done many bad things and that you have sinned greatly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:12 (#2)
content:
רַבִּ֣ים פִּשְׁעֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וַ⁠עֲצֻמִ֖ים חַטֹּֽאתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם

"your transgressions {are} many, and your sins {are} mighty"

The terms transgressions and sins mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [your sins are very many and very great]

See: Doublet

title: Amos 5:12 (#3)
content:
צַדִּיק֙

"the righteous"

Yahweh is using the adjective righteous as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Amos 5:12 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אֶבְיוֹנִ֖ים & הִטּֽוּ

"and they turn aside the needy"

Yahweh is speaking of those who deny justice to poor people as if they physically turn aside the needy so that they cannot reach the gate, the place where legal cases are decided. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they deny justice to the needy]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:12 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אֶבְיוֹנִ֖ים

"the needy"

Amos is using the adjective needy as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [needy people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Amos 5:12 (#6)
content:
בַּ⁠שַּׁ֥עַר

"in the gate"

Here, the gate represents “the place where the leaders of a city decided legal cases.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at the place where legal cases are decided]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:13 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠מַּשְׂכִּ֛יל

"the prudent"

Amos is using the adjective prudent as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wise]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Amos 5:13 (#2)
content:
יִדֹּ֑ם

"will be still"

The word translated as will be still could mean: (1) “will be quiet.” That is, prudent people will avoid criticizing people who do evil because doing so would be futile. Alternate translation: [will be silent] or (2) “will cease.” This would mean that prudent people will cease, that is, that there will be no more prudent people. Alternate translation: [will cease] or [will not be found]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Amos 5:14 (#1)
content:
דִּרְשׁוּ־ט֥וֹב וְ⁠אַל־רָ֖ע

"Seek good, and not evil"

Amos is speaking of trying to do something good or evil as if good and evil were objects someone would actually go search for or seek. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Try to do what is good, and not what is evil]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:14 (#2)
content:
כֵ֞ן

"thus"

The word translated as thus indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [as a result,]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Amos 5:14 (#3)
content:
אֱלֹהֵֽי־צְבָא֛וֹת

"God of Armies"

Amos is using this possessive form to mean the God who commands the armies of heaven. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who commands the armies of heaven]

See: Possession

title: Amos 5:15 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הַצִּ֥יגוּ בַ⁠שַּׁ֖עַר מִשְׁפָּ֑ט

"and establish justice in the gate"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of justice, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and judge fairly in the gate]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַצִּ֥יגוּ בַ⁠שַּׁ֖עַר מִשְׁפָּ֑ט

"and establish justice in the gate"

Here, the gate represents “the place where the leaders of a city decided legal cases.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and establish justice in the place where the city leaders judge legal cases]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:15 (#3)
content:
אוּלַ֗י & יְהוָ֥ה

"perhaps Yahweh"

This part of the verse introduces the possible consequence of fulfilling the condition proposed in the previous part. Use a natural form in your language for introducing the possible consequence of fulfilling this condition. Alternate translation: [if you do all those things, then perhaps, Yahweh]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Amos 5:15 (#4)
content:
אֱלֹהֵֽי־צְבָא֖וֹת

"God of Armies"

See how you translated this same phrase, “God of Armies,” in 5:14.

See: Possession

title: Amos 5:15 (#5)
content:
אוּלַ֗י יֶֽחֱנַ֛ן יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽי־צְבָא֖וֹת

"perhaps Yahweh, God of Armies, will be gracious"

Amos is presenting a possible situation, that Yahweh will be gracious to the survivors of the northern kingdom if the people hate evil, love good, and establish justice. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [if you do these things, then perhaps Yahweh, God of Armies, may be gracious]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Amos 5:15 (#6)
content:
שְׁאֵרִ֥ית יוֹסֵֽף

"to the remnant of Joseph"

Amos is using the possessive form to describe a remnant that is made up of the remaining descendants of Joseph. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to those who survive among the descendants of Joseph]

See: Possession

title: Amos 5:16 (#1)
content:
אֱלֹהֵ֤י צְבָאוֹת֙

"God of Armies"

See how you translated this same phrase, “God of Armies,” in 5:14.

See: Possession

title: Amos 5:16 (#2)
content:
הוֹ־ה֑וֹ

"Alas! Alas"

Yahweh is describing people using a word, Alas, that expresses a strong feeling of dismay and distress. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh no! Oh no!] or [What a disaster!]

See: Exclamations

title: Amos 5:16 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠מִסְפֵּ֖ד אֶל־י֥וֹדְעֵי נֶֽהִי

"and wailing to those knowing a lament"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context of the previous phrase if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will call those knowing a lament to wailing]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 5:17 (#1)
content:
אֶעֱבֹ֥ר בְּ⁠קִרְבְּ⁠ךָ֖

"I will pass through your midst"

Yahweh assumes that readers would understand that the words pass through meant that he would be coming among them to punish them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will come among you and punish you]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 5:17 (#2)
content:
אָמַ֥ר יְהוָֽה

"says Yahweh"

Amos is using the phrase says Yahweh to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 5:18 (#1)
content:
ה֥וֹי הַ⁠מִּתְאַוִּ֖ים

"Woe to the ones desiring"

Amos is using a phrase, Woe to, that expresses a strong feeling of grief and warning about coming disaster. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How dreadful it will be for those desiring]

See: Exclamations

title: Amos 5:18 (#2)
content:
אֶת־י֣וֹם יְהוָ֑ה

"the day of Yahweh"

Amos knows that his readers thought of the day of Yahweh as a time when Yahweh will come to bring justice but they thought it was to judge their enemies, not themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the time when Yahweh will come to bring justice]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 5:18 (#3)
content:
לָ⁠מָּה־זֶּ֥ה לָ⁠כֶ֛ם י֥וֹם יְהוָ֖ה

"What {is} this to you, the day of Yahweh"

Amos is using the question form to rebuke his hearers for wanting the day of Yahweh to come. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The day of Yahweh will bring you no benefit!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 5:18 (#4)
content:
הוּא־חֹ֥שֶׁךְ וְ⁠לֹא־אֽוֹר

"It {is} darkness and not light"

Amos is speaking as if disaster were darkness and deliverance were light. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It is a day of disaster and not of deliverance]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:18 (#5)
content:
הוּא־חֹ֥שֶׁךְ וְ⁠לֹא־אֽוֹר

"It {is} darkness and not light"

The pronoun It refers to the day of Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [That day is darkness and not light]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 5:19 (#1)
content:
כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָנ֥וּס אִישׁ֙ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֲרִ֔י

"As when a man flees from the face of the lion"

The point of this comparison is that just as a man who escapes one deadly danger runs straight into another, so the people of Israel will find no escape when Yahweh judges them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [You will be as unable to escape as a man who flees from the face of the lion]

See: Simile

title: Amos 5:19 (#2)
content:
מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֲרִ֔י

"from the face of the lion"

Here, the face represents “the presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the presence of the lion]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:19 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠פְגָע֖⁠וֹ הַ⁠דֹּ֑ב

"and the bear meets him"

The pronoun him refers to the man who is fleeing from the lion. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the bear meets that man]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 5:19 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠בָ֣א הַ⁠בַּ֔יִת

"or goes into the house"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [or as when a man goes into the house]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 5:19 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠סָמַ֤ךְ יָד⁠וֹ֙ עַל־הַ⁠קִּ֔יר וּ⁠נְשָׁכ֖⁠וֹ הַ⁠נָּחָֽשׁ

"and rests his hand on the wall, and the snake bites him"

The implication is that the man goes into the house in order to be safe, but that even there he meets deadly danger. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [rests his hand on the wall, thinking he is now safe, and the snake bites him]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 5:20 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠לֹא־חֹ֛שֶׁךְ י֥וֹם יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹא־א֑וֹר וְ⁠אָפֵ֖ל וְ⁠לֹא־נֹ֥גַֽהּ לֽ⁠וֹ

"Is} not the day of Yahweh darkness, and not light? Even gloom, with no brightness in it"

Amos is using the question form to emphasize that the day of Yahweh will certainly bring disaster and nothing good. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The day of Yahweh is darkness, and not light, and gloom, with no brightness in it!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 5:20 (#2)
content:
י֥וֹם יְהוָ֖ה

"the day of Yahweh"

See how you translated the similar expression in 5:18.

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:20 (#3)
content:
חֹ֛שֶׁךְ & וְ⁠לֹא־א֑וֹר וְ⁠אָפֵ֖ל וְ⁠לֹא־נֹ֥גַֽהּ

"darkness, and not light? Even gloom, with no brightness"

Amos is speaking as if disaster were darkness and gloom and as if deliverance were light and brightness. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [disaster, and not deliverance? Even sorrow, with no relief]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:20 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אָפֵ֖ל וְ⁠לֹא־נֹ֥גַֽהּ לֽ⁠וֹ

"Even gloom, with no brightness in it"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Is the day of Yahweh not even gloom, with no brightness in it]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 5:21 (#1)
content:
שָׂנֵ֥אתִי מָאַ֖סְתִּי חַגֵּי⁠כֶ֑ם

"I hate, I reject your feasts"

This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh as in the UST.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 5:21 (#2)
content:
שָׂנֵ֥אתִי מָאַ֖סְתִּי

"I hate, I reject"

The terms hate and reject mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I reject with utter hatred]

See: Doublet

title: Amos 5:21 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א אָרִ֖יחַ בְּ⁠עַצְּרֹֽתֵי⁠כֶֽם

"and I will not smell in your assemblies"

Here, Yahweh uses smell to represent his accepting the pleasing aroma of the smoke that ascended from the burnt sacrifices. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will take no pleasure in the sacrifices you offer at your assemblies]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:22 (#1)
content:
כִּ֣י אִם־תַּעֲלוּ־לִ֥⁠י עֹל֛וֹת

"For if you offer up to me burnt offerings"

Yahweh is presenting a possible situation, that the people might offer up to him burnt offerings and grain offerings. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [For suppose you offer up to me burnt offerings]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

title: Amos 5:22 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠שֶׁ֥לֶם מְרִיאֵי⁠כֶ֖ם

"and the peace offering of your fattened animals"

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a peace offering that is made from your fattened animals. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the peace offering that you make from your fattened animals]

See: Possession

title: Amos 5:22 (#3)
content:
לֹ֥א אַבִּֽיט

"I will not look at"

Here, look at represents regarding something with favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will not regard with favor]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:22 (#4)
content:
לֹ֥א אַבִּֽיט

"I will not look at"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will not look at your peace offerings]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 5:23 (#1)
content:
הֲמ֣וֹן שִׁרֶ֑י⁠ךָ

"the noise of your songs"

Here, your songs and the music of your harps represent “the worship that you offer to me.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the noise of the worship you offer me]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:23 (#2)
content:
לֹ֥א אֶשְׁמָֽע

"I will not hear"

Here, hear represents “accept” or “pay attention to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will not accept as worship]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 5:24 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠יִגַּ֥ל כַּ⁠מַּ֖יִם מִשְׁפָּ֑ט

"But let justice roll down like waters"

The point of this comparison is that just as waters flow abundantly and spread everywhere, so justice should be abundant and spread everywhere among the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [But let justice spread everywhere like waters]

See: Simile

title: Amos 5:24 (#2)
content:
מִשְׁפָּ֑ט

"justice"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of justice, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people treating each other justly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:24 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠צְדָקָ֖ה כְּ⁠נַ֥חַל אֵיתָֽן

"and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream"

The point of this comparison is that just as an ever-flowing stream never stops, so righteousness should be constantly among the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and righteousness flowing constantly like a stream that never stops]

See: Simile

title: Amos 5:24 (#4)
content:
וּ⁠צְדָקָ֖ה

"and righteousness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of righteousness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and doing what is right]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 5:25 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠זְּבָחִ֨ים וּ⁠מִנְחָ֜ה הִֽגַּשְׁתֶּם־לִ֧⁠י בַ⁠מִּדְבָּ֛ר אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה

"Did you bring near to me sacrifices and a grain offering in the wilderness forty years"

Yahweh is using the question form to challenge the assumption of the people that sacrifices are all that he requires of them when actually, what he wants is their love and obedience. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You did not bring near to me sacrifices and grain offerings in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 5:25 (#2)
content:
הִֽגַּשְׁתֶּם־לִ֧⁠י

"Did you bring near to me"

The pronoun you refers to the ancestors of the Israelites being addressed who lived during the years in the wilderness. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Did your ancestors bring near to me]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 5:25 (#3)
content:
בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"house of Israel"

See how you translated the similar expression in 5:1.

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 5:26 (#1)
content:
אֵ֚ת סִכּ֣וּת מַלְכְּ⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠אֵ֖ת כִּיּ֣וּן צַלְמֵי⁠כֶ֑ם כּוֹכַב֙ אֱלֹ֣הֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"Sikkuth your king, and Kiyyun your images, the star of your gods"

Sikkuth and Kiyyun are the names of gods that the people of other nations worshiped that the Israelites also worshiped. If your readers would not be familiar with what these are, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the statue of the god you called your king, and the image of another star-god you worshiped]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Amos 5:26 (#2)
content:
אֲשֶׁ֥ר עֲשִׂיתֶ֖ם לָ⁠כֶֽם

"which you made for yourselves"

The pronoun which refers to the images of the gods that the people carried. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [which images of your gods you made for yourselves]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 5:26 (#3)
content:
כּוֹכַב֙ אֱלֹ֣הֵי⁠כֶ֔ם

"the star of your gods"

By the star of your gods, Yahweh is further clarifying that Kiyyun is the false god that they worshiped that is represented by a star. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the god that you worship that is represented by a star]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 5:27 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִגְלֵיתִ֥י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם

"So I will exile you"

The word translated as So indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because you did those things, I will exile you]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Amos 5:27 (#2)
content:
מֵ⁠הָ֣לְאָה לְ⁠דַמָּ֑שֶׂק

"from farther than Damascus"

Yahweh assumes that readers would have known that farther than Damascus represented all the lands far to the north and east, where Assyria rules. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the distant lands ruled by Assyria]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 5:27 (#3)
content:
אֱלֹהֵֽי־צְבָא֖וֹת

"God of Armies"

See how you translated this same phrase, “Yahweh, God of Armies is his name” in 4:13. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who is God of Armies]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos - Chapter 6 Introduction
content:
Amos 6 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a woe oracle against Israel’s complacent leaders (verses 1–7) and Yahweh’s sworn judgment (verses 8–14).

  1. Yahweh warns the complacent and self-confident (1–7)
  2. Yahweh rejects Israel’s pride and luxury (8–11)
  3. Yahweh brings judgment on Israel for its injustice (12–14)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Woe

A woe oracle announces coming disaster in the tone of a funeral lament.

Oath

In verse 8 Yahweh swears by his own soul, since there is no one greater.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Chains of participles

The dashes in verses 3–6 and 13 mark phrases describing the people of verse 1.

title: Amos 6:1 (#1)
content:
ה֚וֹי הַ⁠שַּׁאֲנַנִּ֣ים בְּ⁠צִיּ֔וֹן וְ⁠הַ⁠בֹּטְחִ֖ים בְּ⁠הַ֣ר שֹׁמְר֑וֹן

"Woe to the ones at ease in Zion, and {to} the ones trusting in the mountain of Samaria"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Woe to the ones who feel completely secure in Zion and in Samaria]

See: Parallelism

title: Amos 6:1 (#2)
content:
ה֚וֹי

"Woe to"

Amos is using the word Woe to express a strong feeling of grief and to warn of coming disaster. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Great disaster will come upon]

See: Exclamations

title: Amos 6:1 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠הַ֣ר שֹׁמְר֑וֹן

"in the mountain of Samaria"

Here, the mountain of Samaria refers to the fortified capital city that was built on that mountain, and so it represents the security that its leaders believed they had. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the defenses of the city of Samaria to keep them safe]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 6:1 (#4)
content:
רֵאשִׁ֣ית הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֔ם

"the first of the nations"

The implication of the phrase the first of the nations is that these leaders regarded Israel as the elite of all the nations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the nation that they consider foremost among all nations]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 6:1 (#5)
content:
לָ⁠הֶ֖ם

"to them"

The pronoun them refers to the complacent leaders in Zion and Samaria whom Amos has just described. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to these leaders]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 6:1 (#6)
content:
בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"the house of Israel"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Israel figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the nation of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 6:2 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠טוֹבִים֙ מִן־הַ⁠מַּמְלָכ֣וֹת הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה

"Are} they better than these kingdoms"

The kingdoms of Judah (represented by Zion) and Israel (represented by Samaria) are being compared to the kingdoms represented by the cities named in this verse. Because of the parallel structure of the two questions in this verse, it is most likely that they refers to the cities that have just been named, and that these kingdoms refers to Judah and Israel. Alternate translation: [Are those cities better than your kingdoms]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 6:2 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠טוֹבִים֙ מִן־הַ⁠מַּמְלָכ֣וֹת הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה אִם־רַ֥ב גְּבוּלָ֖⁠ם מִ⁠גְּבֻלְ⁠כֶֽם

"Are} they better than these kingdoms? Or {is} their border greater than your border"

The expected answer to these questions is “No.” The speaker is using the question form to emphasize that Judah and Israel are better in the sense that they are larger and more prosperous than the nations around them. It is possible that Amos is quoting these words from the “designated ones” who are boasting about their kingdoms. But since he refers to your border, it seems more likely that Amos is speaking to the “designated ones” and pointing out that, although God has made their kingdoms great, he will also destroy them because they are not better in the way that they should be. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as exclamations or as statements, as in the UST.

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 6:3 (#1)
content:
הַֽ⁠מְנַדִּ֖ים לְ⁠י֣וֹם רָ֑ע וַ⁠תַּגִּישׁ֖וּ⁠ן

"the ones putting far off the evil day, but you bring near"

Amos begins by speaking about these people in the third person as the ones putting, and then he addresses them directly in the second person with you bring near. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the second person throughout. Alternate translation: [you who put far off the evil day, but bring near]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Amos 6:3 (#2)
content:
הַֽ⁠מְנַדִּ֖ים לְ⁠י֣וֹם רָ֑ע

"the ones putting far off the evil day"

This phrase resumes the description of the people whom Amos pronounced disaster or “woe” upon in 6:1, and that description continues through verse 6. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to repeat the statement about the woe together with the information about these people and beginning a new sentence here. Alternate translation: [Woe to you! You put far off the evil day]

See: Information Structure

title: Amos 6:3 (#3)
content:
הַֽ⁠מְנַדִּ֖ים לְ⁠י֣וֹם רָ֑ע

"the ones putting far off the evil day"

Amos is speaking of these people refusing to think about the coming day of judgment as if that day were an object that they were putting far off, or physically pushing away from themselves. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones pushing away the thought of the evil day] or [the ones refusing to think about the coming day of disaster]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 6:3 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠י֣וֹם רָ֑ע

"the evil day"

Here, Amos is referring to “the day of Yahweh” mentioned in 5:18 as the evil day since it was the time when Yahweh will bring justice by punishing them. Alternate translation: [the day of disaster that Yahweh will bring]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 6:3 (#5)
content:
וַ⁠תַּגִּישׁ֖וּ⁠ן

"but you bring near"

Here Amos is speaking hastening the coming time of violent rule as if that time were an object that could be brought physically near. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but you are hastening the arrival of a time of violence] or [but you are making the time when violent people will rule come sooner]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 6:3 (#6)
content:
שֶׁ֥בֶת חָמָֽס

"a seat of violence"

Here, a seat of represents “a throne” or “a reign of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a reign of violence]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 6:3 (#7)
content:
שֶׁ֥בֶת חָמָֽס

"a seat of violence"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of violence, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a violent rule]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 6:4 (#1)
content:
מִטּ֣וֹת שֵׁ֔ן

"beds of ivory"

Amos is using the possessive form to describe beds that are inlaid with ivory. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [beds decorated with ivory]

See: Possession

title: Amos 6:4 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠עֲגָלִ֖ים מִ⁠תּ֥וֹךְ מַרְבֵּֽק

"and calves from the midst of the stall"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and eating calves from the midst of the stall]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 6:5 (#1)
content:
עַל־פִּ֣י הַ⁠נָּ֑בֶל

"on the mouth of the harp"

Amos is using on the mouth of the harp as a common expression of the culture that means “to the sound of the harp.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the music of the harp]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 6:6 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠רֵאשִׁ֥ית שְׁמָנִ֖ים

"with the first of oils"

Amos is using the first of oils as a common expression of the culture to mean “the finest oils.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the choicest oils]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 6:6 (#2)
content:
שֵׁ֥בֶר יוֹסֵֽף

"the breaking of Joseph"

Amos is speaking as if the coming ruin of the nation were the breaking of an object. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the destruction that is coming upon the descendants of Joseph]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 6:6 (#3)
content:
יוֹסֵֽף

"Joseph"

Here, Joseph represents the people of the northern kingdom of Israel, who were descended from his sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 6:7 (#1)
content:
לָ⁠כֵ֛ן

"Therefore"

The term translated as Therefore indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [As a result]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Amos 6:7 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠רֹ֣אשׁ גֹּלִ֑ים

"at the head of the exiles"

Amos is using at the head of the exiles as a common expression of the culture to mean “first among those who are taken away into exile.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as the first ones to be taken away]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 6:7 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠סָ֖ר מִרְזַ֥ח סְרוּחִֽים

"and the revelry of the sprawling ones will depart"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of revelry, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the ones sprawling out will no longer celebrate loudly]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 6:8 (#1)
content:
נִשְׁבַּע֩ אֲדֹנָ֨⁠י יְהוִ֜ה בְּ⁠נַפְשׁ֗⁠וֹ

"The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his soul"

Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred, in this case by his soul or his own life, since there is no one greater by whom he could swear. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. Alternate translation: [The Lord Yahweh has taken an oath, swearing by his own life]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Amos 6:8 (#2)
content:
אֶת־גְּא֣וֹן יַֽעֲקֹ֔ב

"the pride of Jacob"

The pride of Jacob could refer to: (1) the land of Israel, which would include their strong cities and their luxuries that are mentioned here. See Psalm 47:4. Alternate translation: [this land that Jacob’s people are so proud of] or (2) the fact that the people of Jacob are so proud of themselves. Alternate translation: [that the people of Jacob are so proud]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 6:8 (#3)
content:
בְּ⁠נַפְשׁ֗⁠וֹ

"by his soul"

Here, his soul represents Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by himself]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 6:8 (#4)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י צְבָא֔וֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh, the God of Armies"

See how you translated the similar phrases, “the declaration of the Lord Yahweh, the God of Armies” in 3:13.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 6:8 (#5)
content:
אֶת־גְּא֣וֹן יַֽעֲקֹ֔ב

"the pride of Jacob"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of pride, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [this nation that Jacob’s people are so proud of]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 6:8 (#6)
content:
יַֽעֲקֹ֔ב

"Jacob"

Here, Jacob represents the people of Israel, who were descended from him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 6:8 (#7)
content:
וּ⁠מְלֹאָֽ⁠הּ

"and its fullness"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of fullness, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and everything in it]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 6:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הָיָ֗ה

"And it will happen"

Amos assumes that readers will know that what follows in these two verses are examples of the kinds of things that will happen when Yahweh punishes them. Use a natural way in your language to express examples of things that will happen.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 6:10 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠נְשָׂא֞⁠וֹ דּוֹד֣⁠וֹ וּ⁠מְסָרְפ֗⁠וֹ

"And his kinsman and the one burning him will lift him up"

The pronoun his refers to a man who has died in the house mentioned in the previous verse, and the pronoun him refers to that same dead man. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And a dead man’s kinsman, the one burning that dead man’s body, will lift him up]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 6:10 (#2)
content:
וּ⁠מְסָרְפ֗⁠וֹ

"and the one burning him"

The implication is that this relative will burn the body of the man who has died rather than bury it, since so many people will have died that the usual custom of burial will not be possible. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the one who will cremate his body instead of burying it]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 6:10 (#3)
content:
לְ⁠הוֹצִ֣יא עֲצָמִים֮

"to bring out the bones"

Here, the bones represents the dead body of the man. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to bring out the corpse]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 6:10 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אָמַ֞ר לַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר בְּ⁠יַרְכְּתֵ֥י הַ⁠בַּ֛יִת הַ⁠ע֥וֹד עִמָּ֖⁠ךְ וְ⁠אָמַ֣ר אָ֑פֶס

"and he will say to the one who {is} in the innermost parts of the house, “Is there yet {anyone} with you?” and he will say, “None"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and he will ask the one who is in the innermost parts of the house whether anyone else is still there with him. That man will tell him that there is no one else in the house.]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Amos 6:10 (#5)
content:
הָ֔ס

"Hush"

The relative is using a word that expresses a strong feeling of alarm. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Silence]

See: Exclamations

title: Amos 6:10 (#6)
content:
כִּ֛י לֹ֥א לְ⁠הַזְכִּ֖יר בְּ⁠שֵׁ֥ם יְהוָֽה

"For not to make mention of the name of Yahweh"

The relative is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For we are not allowed to make mention of the name of Yahweh]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 6:11 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠בַּ֥יִת הַ⁠גָּד֖וֹל רְסִיסִ֑ים וְ⁠הַ⁠בַּ֥יִת הַ⁠קָּטֹ֖ן

"the great house into fragments, and the small house"

Amos is referring to all of the houses in the land by naming two extremes, the great house and the small house. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every house]

See: Merism

title: Amos 6:11 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠בַּ֥יִת הַ⁠קָּטֹ֖ן בְּקִעִֽים

"and the small house into fissures"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will strike the small house into fissures]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 6:12 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠יְרֻצ֤וּ⁠ן בַּ⁠סֶּ֨לַע֙ סוּסִ֔ים אִֽם־יַחֲר֖וֹשׁ בַּ⁠בְּקָרִ֑ים

"Do horses run on the cliff? Or does one plow {it} with oxen"

Amos is using the question form to show that what the people of Israel have done is even more absurd than horses running or oxen plowing on a cliff. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Horses certainly do not run on the cliff! No one plows it with oxen!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 6:12 (#2)
content:
הֲפַכְתֶּ֤ם לְ⁠רֹאשׁ֙ מִשְׁפָּ֔ט וּ⁠פְרִ֥י צְדָקָ֖ה לְ⁠לַעֲנָֽה

"you have turned justice into poisonweed, and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood"

Amos is speaking as if justice and righteousness were crops that these people had turned into the bitter and poisonous plants poisonweed and wormwood. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have made justice something deadly, and the results of right behavior something bitter]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 6:12 (#3)
content:
הֲפַכְתֶּ֤ם לְ⁠רֹאשׁ֙ מִשְׁפָּ֔ט

"you have turned justice into poisonweed"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of justice, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you have turned judging people justly into poisonweed]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 6:12 (#4)
content:
לְ⁠רֹאשׁ֙

"into poisonweed"

The term poisonweed refers to a kind of plant that is bitter and poisonous. If your readers would not be familiar with this plant is, you could use the name of a similar plant that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [into something bitter and poisonous]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Amos 6:12 (#5)
content:
וּ⁠פְרִ֥י צְדָקָ֖ה לְ⁠לַעֲנָֽה

"and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and you have turned the fruit of righteousness into bitter wormwood]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 6:12 (#6)
content:
וּ⁠פְרִ֥י צְדָקָ֖ה

"and the fruit of righteousness"

Amos is speaking of righteousness as if it were a plant that could bear fruit, meaning the good results that come from acting righteously. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the good results from acting righteously]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 6:12 (#7)
content:
לְ⁠לַעֲנָֽה

"into wormwood"

The term wormwood refers to a kind of plant that has a very bitter taste. If your readers would not be familiar with what wormwood is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. See how you translated the similar phrase “turning justice into wormwood” in 5:17. Alternate translation: [into a bitter plant]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Amos 6:13 (#1)
content:
לְ⁠לֹ֣א דָבָ֑ר

"over Lo Debar"

Lo Debar is the name of a town. It means, “not a thing.” So although this was a real town that Israel had captured, Amos is also saying that they are rejoicing over nothing. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Amos 6:13 (#2)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא בְ⁠חָזְקֵ֔⁠נוּ לָקַ֥חְנוּ לָ֖⁠נוּ קַרְנָֽיִם

"Have we not by our strength taken Karnaim for ourselves"

These people are using the question form to boast about their own strength. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Indeed, by our own strength we have taken Karnaim for ourselves!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 6:13 (#3)
content:
קַרְנָֽיִם

"Karnaim"

Karnaim is the name of a town. It means, “a pair of horns,” which is a symbol of strength. Amos is implying that just as the strength of Karnaim did not help them, neither should Israel trust in their own strength. Only Yahweh is truly strong. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote.

See: How to Translate Names

title: Amos 6:13 (#4)
content:
הָ⁠אֹ֣מְרִ֔ים הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא בְ⁠חָזְקֵ֔⁠נוּ לָקַ֥חְנוּ לָ֖⁠נוּ קַרְנָֽיִם

"the ones saying, “Have we not by our strength taken Karnaim for ourselves"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [the ones saying that by their strength they have taken Karnaim for themselves]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Amos 6:14 (#1)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִי֩ מֵקִ֨ים

"behold me raising up"

Yahweh is using behold me as a common expression of the culture to mean that the person is about to do something. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to raise up]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 6:14 (#2)
content:
בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל

"house of Israel"

See how you translated the similar expression in 6:1.

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 6:14 (#3)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֛ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י הַ⁠צְּבָא֖וֹת

"the declaration of Yahweh, the God of Armies"

See how you translated the similar phrases, “the declaration of the Lord Yahweh, the God of Armies” in 3:13.

See: Direct and Indirect Quotations

title: Amos 6:14 (#4)
content:
גּ֑וֹי וְ⁠לָחֲצ֥וּ אֶתְ⁠כֶ֛ם

"a nation, and they will oppress you"

In this verse, the word nation is singular in form, but it refers to all of the people of that nation as a group. That is why Yahweh then speaks of that nation with the plural pronoun they. If it would be helpful, you could use a more natural way to express this in your language. Alternate translation: [people of another nation will oppress you]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Amos 6:14 (#5)
content:
מִ⁠לְּב֥וֹא חֲמָ֖ת עַד־נַ֥חַל הָ⁠עֲרָבָֽה

"from Lebo Hamath to the brook of the Arabah"

Yahweh is referring to all of that region by naming two extremes, Lebo Hamath in the far north and the brook of the Arabah in the far south. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout the whole region]

See: Merism

title: Amos - Chapter 7 Introduction
content:
Amos 7 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

Three vision reports, each opening with the same formula, are followed by the narrative of Amaziah’s confrontation with Amos at Bethel (verses 10–17).

  1. Yahweh shows mercy through Amos’s intercession (1–6)
  2. Yahweh measures Israel’s faithfulness and announces judgment (7–9)
  3. Amos faces opposition for proclaiming Yahweh’s word (10–17)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

Prophetic intercession

Amos pleads for Israel after the first two visions and Yahweh relents; after the third vision he does not plead.

The royal sanctuary at Bethel

Bethel was the king’s own sanctuary, so Amaziah treats the message of Amos as a crime against Jeroboam.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

Visions

Each vision repeats some form of this formula: “Thus the Lord Yahweh made me see, and behold….” Notice that in this context, “behold” quite literally means “and see” or “I saw that” since it is a vision that Yahweh is showing Amos. Translate these repeated phrases consistently.

title: Amos 7:1 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הִ֨נֵּה

"And behold"

Amos is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [It was significant that]

See: Foreground Information

title: Amos 7:1 (#2)
content:
אַחַ֖ר גִּזֵּ֥י הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ

"was} after the mowings of the king"

The phrase after the mowings of the king means that the king had the right to take the first cutting of hay from the fields for his own use, so the crop that the locusts were about to eat was all that was left for the people to use for themselves and their animals. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [after the king’s men had cut the first hay for him, so it was the crop the people needed for themselves and their animals]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 7:2 (#1)
content:
כִּלָּה֙

"it had finished"

The pronoun it refers to the locust swarm mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the locust swarm had finished]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 7:2 (#2)
content:
מִ֥י יָק֖וּם יַֽעֲקֹ֑ב

"How will Jacob stand"

Amos is using the question form for emphasis, to express his conviction that the people of Jacob will not be able to survive such a disaster. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Jacob will surely not be able to stand!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 7:2 (#3)
content:
יַֽעֲקֹ֑ב

"Jacob"

Here, Amos is using the name Jacob to refer to the people of Israel who were all descendants of the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the nation of Israel]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:2 (#4)
content:
קָטֹ֖ן

"small"

Amos is speaking of Jacob as if he were physically small. He means that the people of Jacob are weak and would be unable to survive this locust plague. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is weak]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 7:3 (#1)
content:
נִחַ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה עַל־זֹ֑את

"Yahweh relented concerning this"

The pronoun this refers to the destruction by locusts that Yahweh had shown Amos in the vision. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh relented concerning this locust plague]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 7:4 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠תֹּ֨אכַל֙ אֶת־תְּה֣וֹם רַבָּ֔ה וְ⁠אָכְלָ֖ה אֶת־הַ⁠חֵֽלֶק

"And it devoured the great deep and was devouring the portion"

Amos is speaking of the fire as if it were a creature that devoured the waters and the land. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it destroyed the great deep and was destroying the portion]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 7:4 (#2)
content:
אֶת־תְּה֣וֹם רַבָּ֔ה

"the great deep"

By the great deep, Amos means the ocean. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the ocean]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 7:4 (#3)
content:
אֶת־הַ⁠חֵֽלֶק

"the portion"

The implication is that the portion is the land that Yahweh had assigned to the Israelites as their own share. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the land Yahweh had allotted to his people]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 7:5 (#1)
content:
מִ֥י יָק֖וּם יַעֲקֹ֑ב כִּ֥י קָטֹ֖ן הֽוּא

"How will Jacob stand? For he {is} small"

See how you translated these same phrases in verse 2.

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 7:6 (#1)
content:
זֹ֑את

"this"

The pronoun this refers to the destruction by fire that Yahweh had shown Amos in the vision. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh relented concerning this judgment by fire]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 7:7 (#1)
content:
אֲדֹנָ֛⁠י נִצָּ֖ב עַל־חוֹמַ֣ת אֲנָ֑ךְ

"the Lord was standing beside a wall of a plumb line"

Here, the Lord was standing beside a wall of a plumb line represents Yahweh coming to examine his people to see whether they measure up to his standard, just as a builder examines a wall to see whether it is straight. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include this information in a footnote. Alternate translation: [the Lord was standing beside a wall to inspect it, ready to test his people against his standard]

See: Symbolic Language

title: Amos 7:7 (#2)
content:
חוֹמַ֣ת אֲנָ֑ךְ וּ⁠בְ⁠יָד֖⁠וֹ אֲנָֽךְ

"a wall of a plumb line, and in his hand {was} a plumb line"

The word translated as plumb line could mean: (1) a plumb line, as in the ULT and UST or (2) a type of metal called “tin.” Alternate translation: [a tin wall and in his hand was tin]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Amos 7:7 (#3)
content:
חוֹמַ֣ת אֲנָ֑ךְ

"a wall of a plumb line"

Amos is using the possessive form to describe a wall that is characterized by being made perfectly straight by using a plumb line, a builder’s tool made of a string with a heavy weight at the end that hangs straight down, used to check if a wall or structure is completely vertical. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a wall that had been made straight by using a plumb line]

See: Possession

title: Amos 7:8 (#1)
content:
עַמִּ֣⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לֹֽא־אוֹסִ֥יף ע֖וֹד עֲב֥וֹר לֽ⁠וֹ

"my people Israel. I will not again repeat to pass over him"

In this verse, the word him is singular in form, but it refers to all of the Israelites as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “him.” Alternate translation: [my people Israel. I will not again repeat to pass over them]

See: Collective Nouns

title: Amos 7:8 (#2)
content:
אֲנָ֑ךְ & אֲנָךְ֙

"A plumb line & a plumb line"

As in verse 7, also in this verse the word translated as plumb line could mean: (1) a plumb line, as in the ULT and UST or (2) a type of metal called “tin.” Alternate translation: [Tin … tin]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Amos 7:8 (#3)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִ֨י שָׂ֤ם אֲנָךְ֙ בְּ⁠קֶ֨רֶב֙ עַמִּ֣⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"Behold me placing a plumb line in the midst of my people Israel"

Yahweh holding a plumb line was a symbolic action by which he showed that he was going to measure his people’s behavior. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Behold me setting a standard by which I will measure my people Israel]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Amos 7:8 (#4)
content:
הִנְ⁠נִ֨י שָׂ֤ם

"Behold me placing"

Yahweh is using Behold me as a common expression of the culture to mean that he is about to do something. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to place]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 7:8 (#5)
content:
לֹֽא־אוֹסִ֥יף ע֖וֹד עֲב֥וֹר לֽ⁠וֹ

"I will not again repeat to pass over him"

Yahweh is using pass over as a common expression of the culture to mean “overlook their sin.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will no longer forgive their sins]
