See: Idiom

title: Amos 7:9 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠נָשַׁ֨מּוּ֙ בָּמ֣וֹת יִשְׂחָ֔ק וּ⁠מִקְדְּשֵׁ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל יֶחֱרָ֑בוּ

"And the high places of Isaac will be deserted, and the sanctuaries of Israel will be desolate"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And all the worship places of the Israelites will surely be left in ruins]

See: Parallelism

title: Amos 7:9 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠נָשַׁ֨מּוּ֙ בָּמ֣וֹת יִשְׂחָ֔ק

"And the high places of Isaac will be deserted"

The expression will be deserted is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I will destroy the high places of Isaac so they will be deserted]

See: Active or Passive

title: Amos 7:9 (#3)
content:
בָּמ֣וֹת יִשְׂחָ֔ק

"the high places of Isaac"

Here, the high places represent the shrines that the Israelites built on hilltops for worshiping idols. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the idolatrous places where the Israelites worshiped]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:9 (#4)
content:
יִשְׂחָ֔ק

"Isaac"

Here, Isaac represents all the people of Israel, as they were all descended from Isaac. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:9 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠קַמְתִּ֛י עַל

"and I will rise against"

Here Yahweh is speaking of sending enemies to fight against them as if he would physically rise. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will attack]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 7:9 (#6)
content:
בֵּ֥ית יָרָבְעָ֖ם

"the house of Jeroboam"

Here, the house of Jeroboam represents “the royal family descended from Jeroboam.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the royal line of those descended from Jeroboam]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:9 (#7)
content:
בֶּ⁠חָֽרֶב

"with the sword"

Here, the sword represents “warfare.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with warfare]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:10 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֗ח אֲמַצְיָה֙ כֹּהֵ֣ן בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל אֶל־יָרָבְעָ֥ם מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"Then Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, sent to Jeroboam, king of Israel"

Amos is introducing Amaziah, the priest of Bethel as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation.

See: Introduction of New and Old Participants

resource.label: Introduction of New and Old Participants

title: Amos 7:10 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֗ח אֲמַצְיָה֙ כֹּהֵ֣ן בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל אֶל־יָרָבְעָ֥ם

"Then Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, sent to Jeroboam"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Then Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, sent a message to Jeroboam]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 7:10 (#3)
content:
בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"the house of Israel"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Israel figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 7:10 (#4)
content:
לֹא־תוּכַ֣ל הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ לְ⁠הָכִ֖יל אֶת־כָּל־דְּבָרָֽי⁠ו

"The land is not able to contain all of his words"

Amaziah says The land is not able to contain all of his words as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [The people of this land cannot endure everything he is saying]

See: Hyperbole

title: Amos 7:11 (#1)
content:
כִּי־כֹה֙ אָמַ֣ר עָמ֔וֹס בַּ⁠חֶ֖רֶב יָמ֣וּת יָרָבְעָ֑ם

"For thus Amos says, ‘By the sword Jeroboam will die"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [For Amos says that Jeroboam will die by the sword]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Amos 7:11 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠חֶ֖רֶב יָמ֣וּת יָרָבְעָ֑ם

"By the sword Jeroboam will die"

Here, the sword represents violent death in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Jeroboam will die violently in battle]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:11 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠יִ֨שְׂרָאֵ֔ל

"and Israel"

Here, Israel represents the nation of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the Israelites]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:11 (#4)
content:
גָּלֹ֥ה יִגְלֶ֖ה

"going into exile, will go into exile"

Amos is repeating forms of the verb go into exile in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [will certainly be taken far away into exile]

See: Reduplication

title: Amos 7:12 (#1)
content:
וֶ⁠אֱכָל־שָׁ֣ם לֶ֔חֶם

"and eat bread there"

Amaziah is using eat bread there as a common expression of the culture to mean to earn what one needs to be able to eat. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and make your living there]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 7:12 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֲמַצְיָה֙ אֶל־עָמ֔וֹס

"And Amaziah said to Amos"

Even though Amos has been speaking of himself in the first person as “I” and “me”, here he switches to speaking of himself in the third person as Amos to recount the exchange with Amaziah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person for consistency. Alternate translation: [And Amaziah said to me]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Amos 7:13 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠בֵֽית־אֵ֔ל לֹֽא־תוֹסִ֥יף ע֖וֹד לְ⁠הִנָּבֵ֑א כִּ֤י מִקְדַּשׁ־מֶ֨לֶךְ֙ ה֔וּא וּ⁠בֵ֥ית מַמְלָכָ֖ה הֽוּא

"But {at} Bethel you shall not repeat to prophesy again, for it {is} a sanctuary of the king, and it {is} a house of a kingdom"

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [But because it is a sanctuary of the king and it is a house of a kingdom, at Bethel you shall not repeat to prophesy again]

See: Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship

title: Amos 7:13 (#2)
content:
לֹֽא־תוֹסִ֥יף ע֖וֹד לְ⁠הִנָּבֵ֑א

"you shall not repeat to prophesy again"

Amaziah is using you shall not repeat to prophesy again as a common expression of the culture to mean “you must not prophesy any more.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you must never prophesy any more]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 7:13 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בֵ֥ית מַמְלָכָ֖ה הֽוּא

"and it {is} a house of a kingdom"

The implication is that by using the phrasea house of a kingdom which implies a royal temple, Amaziah is claiming that Bethel is a temple of the northern kingdom of Israel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and it is the royal temple of the northern kingdom of Israel]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 7:14 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֤עַן עָמוֹס֙ וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל־אֲמַצְיָ֔ה

"And Amos answered and said to Amaziah"

As in verse 12, Amos is speaking of himself in the third person as Amos. If you chose to translate it in the first person there, you should do so here as well. Alternate translation: [And I answered and said to Amaziah]

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Amos 7:14 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יַּ֤עַן עָמוֹס֙ וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר

"And Amos answered and said"

The terms answered and said together introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent both terms explicitly as modeled in the UST.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 7:14 (#3)
content:
לֹא־נָבִ֣יא אָנֹ֔כִי וְ⁠לֹ֥א בֶן־נָבִ֖יא אָנֹ֑כִי כִּֽי־בוֹקֵ֥ר אָנֹ֖כִי

"I {am} not a prophet, and I {am} not a son of a prophet, for I {am} a herdsman"

Since this verse has no verbs in the original, this could mean: (1) that Amos is not currently a professional prophet or part of a group of prophets but a herdsman, as modeled in the UST and UST or (2) that Amos was a herdsman and not a prophet before Yahweh called him to prophesy. Alternate translation: [I was not a prophet, and I was not a son of a prophet, for I was a herdsman]

title: Amos 7:14 (#4)
content:
לֹא־נָבִ֣יא אָנֹ֔כִי וְ⁠לֹ֥א בֶן־נָבִ֖יא אָנֹ֑כִי

"I {am} not a prophet, and I {am} not a son of a prophet"

Amos is using a son of a prophet as a common expression of the culture to mean “a disciple of a prophet.” He is making a point that he did not make his living as a prophet as those who were considered part of the official group of prophets did. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.

See: Idiom

title: Amos 7:14 (#5)
content:
שִׁקְמִֽים

"sycamore figs"

The term sycamore figs describes a kind of fruit that grows on a large tree that was common in the warm, low-lying areas of that region. If your readers would not be familiar with what sycamore figs are, you could use the name of a similar fruit that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a kind of fig]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Amos 7:15 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠יִּקָּחֵ֣⁠נִי יְהוָ֔ה מֵ⁠אַחֲרֵ֖י הַ⁠צֹּ֑אן

"But Yahweh took me from after the flock"

Amos is using took me from after the flock as a common expression of the culture to mean “took me away from tending sheep.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh took me away from my work of caring for the sheep]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 7:15 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלַ⁠י֙ יְהוָ֔ה לֵ֥ךְ הִנָּבֵ֖א אֶל־עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

"and Yahweh said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh told me to go prophesy to his people Israel]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Amos 7:16 (#1)
content:
דְּבַר־יְהוָ֑ה

"the word of Yahweh"

Here, the word of Yahweh represents the message that Yahweh is speaking through Amos. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the message that Yahweh has for me to give you]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:16 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֥א תַטִּ֖יף

"and you shall not drip"

Amaziah is speaking of prophesying or preaching as if it were words that drip from the prophet’s mouth, letting words fall like rain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you shall not preach]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 7:16 (#3)
content:
בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂחָֽק

"the house of Isaac"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Isaac means all the people descended from the patriarch Isaac which is all the people of Israel. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 7:17 (#1)
content:
אִשְׁתְּ⁠ךָ֞ בָּ⁠עִ֤יר תִּזְנֶה֙

"Your wife will prostitute herself in the city"

The implication is that enemy soldiers will capture the city and force Amaziah’s wife to become a prostitute. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Your wife will be forced to become a prostitute in the city when enemy soldiers capture it]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 7:17 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אַדְמָתְ⁠ךָ֖ בַּ⁠חֶ֣בֶל תְּחֻלָּ֑ק

"and your ground will be divided by the measuring line"

The expression will be divided is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and enemies will divide your ground with the measuring line]

See: Active or Passive

title: Amos 7:17 (#3)
content:
בַּ⁠חֶ֣בֶל

"by the measuring line"

Here, the measuring line represents “the parceling out of land to new owners,” since people used such a line to mark off the boundaries of property. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into parcels for new owners]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 7:17 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אַתָּ֗ה עַל־אֲדָמָ֤ה טְמֵאָה֙ תָּמ֔וּת

"and you, you will die on unclean ground"

The implication is that unclean ground is a foreign land where people worship other gods, so that it is not a fit place for a worshiper of Yahweh to live. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and you, you will die in a foreign land that is defiled by the worship of other gods]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 7:17 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠אַתָּ֗ה & תָּמ֔וּת

"and you, you will die"

Amos is stating the pronoun you separately, even though the verb translated as you will die already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is now address Amaziah’s own fate. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and you, yourself will die]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 7:17 (#6)
content:
גָּלֹ֥ה יִגְלֶ֖ה

"going into exile, will go into exile"

See how you translated the similar expression in 7:11.

See: Reduplication

title: Amos - Chapter 8 Introduction
content:
Amos 8 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

  1. Yahweh announces the end of Israel (1–3)
  2. Yahweh condemns Israel’s greed and injustice (4–8)
  3. Yahweh brings darkness and famine for his word (9–14)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The new moon and the Sabbath

Israelites did not trade on these holy days, so the merchants in verse 5 are impatient for them to end.

Translation Issues in This Chapter

A famine of Yahweh’s words

In verses 11–13, hunger and thirst are used figuratively for Yahweh withholding his word.

Vision

This chapter begins with another vision. Be sure use language consistent with introducing the visions in the previous chapter, “Thus the Lord Yahweh made me see, and behold….” Notice that in this context, “behold” quite literally means “and see” or “I saw that” since it is a vision that Yahweh is showing Amos.

title: Amos 8:2 (#1)
content:
קָ֑יִץ

"summer fruit"

The word translated as summer fruit sounds very much like the word for end. Yahweh’s purpose in showing Amos summer fruit was to give him a prophecy of the end of his people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 8:2 (#2)
content:
לֹא־אוֹסִ֥יף ע֖וֹד עֲב֥וֹר לֽ⁠וֹ

"I will not repeat again to pass over him"

See how you translated this same phrase in 7:8.

See: Idiom

title: Amos 8:3 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הֵילִ֜ילוּ שִׁיר֤וֹת הֵיכָל֙

"And the songs of the temple will wail"

Here, the songs of the temple represents “the people who sing the songs in the temple.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the singers in the temple will wail]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:3 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֔וּא

"in that day"

The phrase in that day refers to that time when Yahweh will punish them, also referred to as “the day of Yahweh” in chapter 5. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the time when I punish you]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:3 (#3)
content:
נְאֻ֖ם אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֑ה

"the declaration of the Lord Yahweh"

Amos, who is conveying Yahweh’s words here, is interjecting the declaration of the Lord Yahweh to emphasize that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 8:3 (#4)
content:
הָֽס

"Hush"

Yahweh is using a word that expresses a strong feeling of dread. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Say nothing, for the dread is too great]

See: Exclamations

title: Amos 8:3 (#5)
content:
הִשְׁלִ֥יךְ

"one has thrown {them"

The pronoun one does not refer to any particular person. It refers to people in general. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [people have thrown]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 8:4 (#1)
content:
הַ⁠שֹּׁאֲפִ֖ים אֶבְי֑וֹן

"the ones trampling the needy"

Amos is speaking of these people oppressing needy people as if they were trampling them underfoot. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones oppressing the needy]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 8:4 (#2)
content:
אֶבְי֑וֹן

"the needy"

Amos is using the adjective needy as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are needy people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Amos 8:4 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠לַ⁠שְׁבִּ֖ית ענוי־אָֽרֶץ

"and to cause the afflicted of the land to cease"

By cause the afflicted of the land to cease, Amos means that they brought about the ruin of the poor because of their unfair treatment which afflicted them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and bring to ruin the afflicted of the land]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 8:4 (#4)
content:
ענוי־אָֽרֶץ

"the afflicted of the land"

Amos is using the adjective afflicted as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the afflicted people of the land]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Amos 8:5 (#1)
content:
מָתַ֞י יַעֲבֹ֤ר הַ⁠חֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ וְ⁠נַשְׁבִּ֣ירָה שֶּׁ֔בֶר וְ⁠הַ⁠שַּׁבָּ֖ת וְ⁠נִפְתְּחָה־בָּ֑ר

"When will the new moon pass, that we may sell grain, and the Sabbath, that we may open wheat"

The implication is that the Israelites were not permitted to buy and sell on the festival of the new moon or on the Sabbath, and so these merchants were impatient for those days to end. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When will the new moon festival, on which we are not allowed to trade, be over, so that we may sell grain, and when will the Sabbath, on which we are also forbidden to trade, be over, so that we may open our bins of wheat]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 8:5 (#2)
content:
לְ⁠הַקְטִ֤ין אֵיפָה֙ וּ⁠לְ⁠הַגְדִּ֣יל שֶׁ֔קֶל

"to make the ephah small and to make the shekel great"

The implication is that these merchants would measure out grain in a container smaller than a standard ephah and weigh their customers’ silver with a weight heavier than a standard shekel, so that they cheated the people who bought from them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to use an undersized ephah measure for grain and an oversized shekel weight for silver]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 8:5 (#3)
content:
מֹאזְנֵ֥י מִרְמָֽה

"balances of deceit"

Amos is using the possessive form to describe balances that are characterized by deceit. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deceitful balances]

See: Possession

title: Amos 8:6 (#1)
content:
לִ⁠קְנ֤וֹת בַּ⁠כֶּ֨סֶף֙ דַּלִּ֔ים וְ⁠אֶבְי֖וֹן בַּ⁠עֲב֣וּר נַעֲלָ֑יִם

"to buy the poor with silver and the needy in exchange for a pair of sandals"

The merchants are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to buy the poor as slaves with silver and to buy the needy as slaves in exchange for a pair of sandals]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 8:6 (#2)
content:
בַּ⁠כֶּ֨סֶף֙ דַּלִּ֔ים וְ⁠אֶבְי֖וֹן

"the poor with silver and the needy"

The merchants are using the adjectives poor and needy as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [poor people with silver and needy people]

See: Nominal Adjectives

title: Amos 8:6 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אֶבְי֖וֹן בַּ⁠עֲב֣וּר נַעֲלָ֑יִם

"and the needy in exchange for a pair of sandals"

The implication is that a pair of sandals would only cost a very small amount. This means that they were buying needy people as slaves for a price as low as the price of a pair of sandals. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the needy for as little as the price of a pair of sandals]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 8:7 (#1)
content:
בִּ⁠גְא֣וֹן יַעֲקֹ֑ב

"by the pride of Jacob"

As in 6:8, the pride of Jacob could refer to: (1) the land of Israel, since that is its meaning elsewhere, and it would make no sense to swear by something negative, such as sinful pride. Alternate translation: [by this land that Jacob’s people are so proud of] or (2) Yahweh himself. This would then be equivalent to the phrase in 6:8, “The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his soul.” Alternate translation: [by himself, of whom Jacob’s people are so proud]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:7 (#2)
content:
יַעֲקֹ֑ב

"Jacob"

Here, Jacob represents the descendants of Jacob, the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Jacob’s descendants]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:7 (#3)
content:
אִם־אֶשְׁכַּ֥ח לָ⁠נֶ֖צַח כָּל־מַעֲשֵׂי⁠הֶֽם

"If I ever forget all of their deeds"

Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”), which would be the penalty for not telling the truth. Normally the penalty would be understood to be something general such as “may Yahweh punish me severely,” yielding something like, “If I ever forget…, then may Yahweh punish me severely…” But since Yahweh is speaking, stating this would not make sense. It may be clearest to translate the oath as a positive statement, as in the UST.

See: Oath Formulas

title: Amos 8:8 (#1)
content:
הַ֤⁠עַל זֹאת֙ לֹֽא־תִרְגַּ֣ז הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠אָבַ֖ל כָּל־יוֹשֵׁ֣ב בָּ֑⁠הּ

"Will not the land tremble over this, and everyone dwelling in it mourn"

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the land will certainly tremble and that everyone living in it will certainly mourn. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The land will surely tremble over this, and everyone dwelling in it will mourn!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 8:8 (#2)
content:
זֹאת֙

"this"

The pronoun this refers to the deeds of the people that Yahweh mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will not the land tremble over the evil deeds that the people have done]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 8:8 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠עָלְתָ֤ה כָ⁠אֹר֙ כֻּלָּ֔⁠הּ וְ⁠נִגְרְשָׁ֥ה ו⁠נשקה כִּ⁠יא֥וֹר מִצְרָֽיִם

"And all of it will rise like the Nile, and be cast up and sunk, like the Nile of Egypt"

The point of this comparison is that just as the Nile of Egypt rises in flood and then sinks back down again, so the whole land of Israel will heave up and down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And the whole land will heave upward and then settle back down, just as the Nile of Egypt rises in flood and then recedes]

See: Simile

title: Amos 8:9 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֗וּא

"in that day"

The phrase in that day refers to that time when Yahweh will punish them. See how you translated this same phrase in verse 3.

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:9 (#2)
content:
נְאֻם֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י

"the declaration of the Lord"

Amos, who is conveying Yahweh’s words here, is interjecting the declaration of the Lord to emphasize that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 8:9 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הֵבֵאתִ֥י הַ⁠שֶּׁ֖מֶשׁ בַּֽ⁠צָּהֳרָ֑יִם וְ⁠הַחֲשַׁכְתִּ֥י לָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ בְּ⁠י֥וֹם אֽוֹר

"that I will make the sun set at noon, and I will darken the land in a day of light"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional as in the UST. Another approach would be to combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [that I will make the sunlight completely disappear in the middle of the day]

See: Parallelism

title: Amos 8:10 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠הַעֲלֵיתִ֤י עַל־כָּל־מָתְנַ֨יִם֙ שָׂ֔ק וְ⁠עַל־כָּל־רֹ֖אשׁ קָרְחָ֑ה

"And I will bring up sackcloth on all loins, and baldness on every head"

Wearing sackcloth and shaving the head were a symbolic actions by which Yahweh’s people would show that they were mourning and grieving. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And I will cause everyone to put on sackcloth around their waists and to shave their heads bald to show their grief]

See: Symbolic Action

title: Amos 8:10 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֨י⁠הָ֙ כְּ⁠אֵ֣בֶל יָחִ֔יד וְ⁠אַחֲרִיתָ֖⁠הּ כְּ⁠י֥וֹם מָֽר

"And I will make it like the mourning for an only child, and its end like a bitter day"

The point of these comparisons is that just as the death of an only child brings parents the deepest possible grief, and just as a bitter day brings the greatest sorrow, so the people of Israel will grieve when Yahweh punishes them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And I will cause you to grieve as deeply as parents who mourn the death of their only child, and everything will end in the most bitter sorrow]

See: Simile

title: Amos 8:11 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֣ה

"Behold"

Yahweh is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention, for]

See: Foreground Information

title: Amos 8:11 (#2)
content:
נְאֻם֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֔ה

"the declaration of the Lord Yahweh"

Amos is interjecting the phrase the declaration of the Lord Yahweh to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 8:11 (#3)
content:
רָעָ֖ב בָּ⁠אָ֑רֶץ לֹֽא־רָעָ֤ב לַ⁠לֶּ֨חֶם֙ וְ⁠לֹֽא־צָמָ֣א לַ⁠מַּ֔יִם כִּ֣י אִם־לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֔עַ אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י יְהוָֽה

"a famine in the land, not a famine for bread, and not a thirst for water, but rather to hear the words of Yahweh"

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [it will not be a famine for food and it will not be a thirst for water, but rather I will send a thirst to hear the words of Yahweh]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 8:12 (#1)
content:
מִ⁠יָּ֣ם עַד־יָ֔ם וּ⁠מִ⁠צָּפ֖וֹן וְ⁠עַד־מִזְרָ֑ח

"from sea to sea, and from the north and to the sunrise"

Yahweh is referring to all of the land by naming the extremes, from sea to sea and from the north and to the sunrise. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in every direction throughout the whole land]

See: Merism

title: Amos 8:12 (#2)
content:
מִזְרָ֑ח

"the sunrise"

Here, the sunrise represents “east.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:13 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֨וֹם הַ⁠ה֜וּא

"In that day"

See how you translated the same phrase, “in that day,” in verse 3. Alternate translation: [At the time when I punish you]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:13 (#2)
content:
תִּ֠תְעַלַּפְנָה הַ⁠בְּתוּלֹ֧ת הַ⁠יָּפ֛וֹת וְ⁠הַ⁠בַּחוּרִ֖ים

"the beautiful virgins will faint, and the young men"

Yahweh is using the beautiful virgins and the young men, to represent the strongest and healthiest of the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [even the strongest among the people, will faint]

See: Synecdoche

title: Amos 8:13 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠הַ⁠בַּחוּרִ֖ים בַּ⁠צָּמָֽא

"and the young men, from thirst"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the young men will faint from thirst]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 8:14 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠אַשְׁמַ֣ת שֹֽׁמְר֔וֹן

"by the guilt of Samaria"

Here, the guilt of Samaria represents the sin of idolatry practiced by the people there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by the idolatry in Samaria that made the people guilty]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:14 (#2)
content:
בְּ⁠אַשְׁמַ֣ת שֹֽׁמְר֔וֹן

"by the guilt of Samaria"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of guilt, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by what makes Samaria guilty]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 8:14 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠אָמְר֗וּ חֵ֤י אֱלֹהֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ דָּ֔ן וְ⁠חֵ֖י דֶּ֣רֶךְ בְּאֵֽר־שָׁ֑בַע

"and they say, ‘By the life of your god, Dan!’ and, ‘By the life of the way of Beersheba"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation as modeled in the UST.

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Amos 8:14 (#4)
content:
חֵ֤י אֱלֹהֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ דָּ֔ן

"By the life of your god, Dan"

Following the custom of the culture, these people are swearing an oath by naming something that they hold sacred when they say By the life of your god, Dan. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. Alternate translation: [As surely as your god lives, Dan]

See: Oath Formulas

title: Amos 8:14 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠חֵ֖י דֶּ֣רֶךְ בְּאֵֽר־שָׁ֑בַע

"and, ‘By the life of the way of Beersheba"

Here, by the life of the way of Beersheba represents the god that people traveled to worship at Beersheba. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and, ‘As surely as the god lives that people go on pilgrimage to worship at Beersheba]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 8:14 (#6)
content:
וְ⁠נָפְל֖וּ וְ⁠לֹא־יָק֥וּמוּ עֽוֹד

"and they will fall, and they will not rise again"

Yahweh is speaking of these people being destroyed with no hope of recovery as if they would fall down and never rise again. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will be destroyed, and they will never recover]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos - Chapter 9 Introduction
content:
Amos 9 Chapter Introduction

Structure and Formatting

  1. Yahweh brings judgment on Israel (1–6)
  2. Yahweh judges Israel among the nations (7–10)
  3. Yahweh restores David’s fallen house and blesses his people (11–15)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

The booth of David

The fallen booth of David in 9:11 pictures his ruined dynasty, which Yahweh will rebuild.

title: Amos 9:1 (#1)
content:
רָאִ֨יתִי אֶת־אֲדֹנָ֜⁠י נִצָּ֣ב עַֽל־הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֗חַ

"I saw the Lord standing by the altar"

Amos is using the words translated as I saw the Lord standing by the altar to introduce a new vision that Yahweh showed him. Use a word or phrase in your language to make that clear.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Amos 9:1 (#2)
content:
הַ⁠כַּפְתּ֜וֹר

"the capital"

A capital is the block of stone at the top of a column or pillar, on which the roof of a building rests. If your readers would not be familiar with what a capital is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the top of the temple columns]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Amos 9:1 (#3)
content:
וּ⁠בְצַ֨עַ⁠ם֙ בְּ⁠רֹ֣אשׁ כֻּלָּ֔⁠ם

"and cut them off on the head of all of them"

The pronoun them refers to the pillars and thresholds, while the phrase all of them refers to the people who are worshiping in the temple. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and make the pieces of the pillars fall on the heads of all the worshipers]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 9:1 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠אַחֲרִיתָ֖⁠ם

"and their end"

Here, their end represents all the rest of the people who were not killed by the collapse of the temple. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and all who are left]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 9:1 (#5)
content:
בַּ⁠חֶ֣רֶב אֶהֱרֹ֑ג

"I will kill with the sword"

Here, the sword represents warfare, that is, attack by an enemy army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will direct their enemies to kill them]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 9:1 (#6)
content:
לֹֽא־יָנ֤וּס לָ⁠הֶם֙ נָ֔ס וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִמָּלֵ֥ט לָ⁠הֶ֖ם פָּלִֽיט

"A fleeing one will not flee for them, and a fugitive will not escape for them"

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way as in the UST. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [A fleeing one will not flee for them, indeed a fugitive will not escape for them]

See: Parallelism

title: Amos 9:2 (#1)
content:
יָדִ֣⁠י תִקָּחֵ֑⁠ם

"my hand will take them"

Here, my hand represents the power of the Lord to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will powerfully take them]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 9:2 (#2)
content:
אִם־יַחְתְּר֣וּ בִ⁠שְׁא֔וֹל מִ⁠שָּׁ֖ם יָדִ֣⁠י תִקָּחֵ֑⁠ם

"If they dig into Sheol, from there my hand will take them"

Here and in the next verse, Amos lists a series of an unreal, hypothetical situations that make the point that no matter where the people would try to hide themselves in order to escape Yahweh’s judgment, Yahweh will still find and punish them. Use a natural method in your language for introducing an imaginary situation. Alternate translation: [Even if they could dig way down into Sheol, from there my hand would take them]

See: Hypothetical Situations

title: Amos 9:3 (#1)
content:
בְּ⁠רֹ֣אשׁ הַ⁠כַּרְמֶ֔ל

"in the head of Carmel"

Here, the head represents the top of the mountain called Carmel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at the summit of Carmel]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 9:3 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠אִם־יִסָּ֨תְר֜וּ מִ⁠נֶּ֤גֶד עֵינַ⁠י֙ בְּ⁠קַרְקַ֣ע הַ⁠יָּ֔ם

"And if they are hidden from before my eyes in the floor of the sea"

The expression are hidden is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And if they hide themselves from before my eyes in the floor of the sea]

See: Active or Passive

title: Amos 9:4 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠אִם־יֵלְכ֤וּ בַ⁠שְּׁבִי֙ לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י אֹֽיבֵי⁠הֶ֔ם

"And if they go in captivity to the face of their enemies"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of captivity, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And if their enemies capture them and carry them off]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 9:4 (#2)
content:
לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י אֹֽיבֵי⁠הֶ֔ם

"to the face of their enemies"

Here, to the face of represents being in the presence of or in front of those enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of their enemies]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 9:4 (#3)
content:
אֲצַוֶּ֥ה אֶת־הַ⁠חֶ֖רֶב וַ⁠הֲרָגָ֑תַ⁠ם

"I will command the sword and it will kill them"

Here, the sword represents the enemies who would use swords to kill them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will command their enemies and they will kill them]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 9:4 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֨י עֵינִ֧⁠י עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם

"And I will set my eye on them"

The Lord is using I will set my eye on them as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will watch them closely,” usually in a positive sense of caring for them but here it is reversed in that it means he is watching them in order to harm them and not to help them. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will watch them closely]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 9:4 (#5)
content:
לְ⁠רָעָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א לְ⁠טוֹבָֽה

"for evil and not for good"

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of evil and good, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [to punish them and not to benefit them]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 9:5 (#1)
content:
וַ⁠אדֹנָ֨⁠י יְהוִ֜ה הַ⁠צְּבָא֗וֹת

"And the Lord Yahweh of Armies"

Amos is using the possessive form the Lord Yahweh of Armies to describe Yahweh as the one who commands the armies of heaven. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Lord Yahweh, who commands the armies of heaven]

See: Possession

title: Amos 9:5 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠עָלְתָ֤ה כַ⁠יְאֹר֙ כֻּלָּ֔⁠הּ וְ⁠שָׁקְעָ֖ה כִּ⁠יאֹ֥ר מִצְרָֽיִם

"and all of it goes up like the Nile, and it sinks like the Nile of Egypt"

See how you translated the very similar phrases in Amos 8:8.

See: Simile

title: Amos 9:6 (#1)
content:
מעלות⁠ו

"his stairs"

The word translated as stairs represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Some scholars have proposed, however, that a scribe may have added an extra letter to this word. Without the extra letter, it would say “upper rooms,” which is how some modern versions translate. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [his upper rooms]

See: Alternative Readings

title: Amos 9:6 (#2)
content:
וַ⁠אֲגֻדָּת֖⁠וֹ

"and his vault"

A vault is a kind of arched or domed roof. Amos uses the term to describe the sky as a dome stretched over the earth. If your readers would not be familiar with what a vault is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and the sky]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Amos 9:6 (#3)
content:
הַ⁠קֹּרֵ֣א לְ⁠מֵֽי־הַ⁠יָּ֗ם וַֽ⁠יִּשְׁפְּכֵ֛⁠ם עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ יְהוָ֥ה שְׁמֽ⁠וֹ

"the one calling to the waters of the sea, and he pours them out upon the face of the earth— Yahweh {is} his name"

See how you translated these very similar phrases in 5:8.

title: Amos 9:7 (#1)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא כִ⁠בְנֵי֩ כֻשִׁיִּ֨ים אַתֶּ֥ם לִ֛⁠י בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"Are you not like the sons of the Cushites to me, sons of Israel"

Yahweh is using the question form to insist that the Israelites are no longer more privileged in his sight than any of these other people groups because they have broken their special covenant with him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You are just like the sons of the Cushites to me, sons of Israel!]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 9:7 (#2)
content:
כִ⁠בְנֵי֩ כֻשִׁיִּ֨ים & לִ֛⁠י בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל

"like the sons of the Cushites to me, sons of Israel"

Yahweh is speaking as if the people of the nation of Cush, which is modern day Ethiopia, were actually the sons of Cush who was the son of Ham, and the people of Israel where the actual sons of the patriarch, Israel. Alternate translation: [like the Cushite people to me, you people of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 9:7 (#3)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

Amos, who is conveying Yahweh’s words, is interjecting the declaration of Yahweh to emphasize that what is being said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 9:7 (#4)
content:
הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל הֶעֱלֵ֨יתִי֙ מֵ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם וּ⁠פְלִשְׁתִּיִּ֥ים מִ⁠כַּפְתּ֖וֹר וַ⁠אֲרָ֥ם מִ⁠קִּֽיר

"Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor, and Aram from Kir"

Yahweh is using the question form to remind the Israelites that he is the one who controls where nations come and go just as he brought Israel out of Egypt. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Not only did I bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, but I also brought the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir.]

See: Rhetorical Question

title: Amos 9:8 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֞ה

"Behold"

Amos is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention!]

See: Foreground Information

title: Amos 9:8 (#2)
content:
עֵינֵ֣י ׀ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֗ה בַּ⁠מַּמְלָכָה֙ הַֽ⁠חַטָּאָ֔ה

"the eyes of the Lord Yahweh are on the sinful kingdom"

Here, the eyes of the Lord Yahweh represents his watchful attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Lord Yahweh is watching the sinful kingdom closely]

See: Metonymy

title: Amos 9:8 (#3)
content:
אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֗ה

"the Lord Yahweh"

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as the Lord Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person as in the UST.

See: First, Second or Third Person

title: Amos 9:8 (#4)
content:
פְּנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֲדָמָ֑ה

"the face of the ground"

Yahweh is using the face of the ground as a common expression of the culture to mean “the surface of the earth” or “the whole earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the surface of the earth] or [the earth]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 9:8 (#5)
content:
אֶ֗פֶס כִּ֠י לֹ֣א הַשְׁמֵ֥יד אַשְׁמִ֛יד אֶת־בֵּ֥ית יַעֲקֹ֖ב

"Nevertheless, destroying, I will not destroy the house of Jacob"

Yahweh uses the word Nevertheless here to indicate a contrast between the destruction of the sinful northern kingdom and his promise to preserve a remnant from the descendants of Jacob. The fact that he will preserve a remnant is evident in the context of the next verse. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But destroying, I will not destroy the entire house of Jacob]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

title: Amos 9:8 (#6)
content:
לֹ֣א הַשְׁמֵ֥יד אַשְׁמִ֛יד

"destroying, I will not destroy"

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb destroy in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I will certainly not completely destroy]

See: Reduplication

title: Amos 9:8 (#7)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

Amos, who is conveying Yahweh’s words, is once again interjecting the declaration of Yahweh to emphasize that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 9:8 (#8)
content:
אֶת־בֵּ֥ית יַעֲקֹ֖ב

"the house of Jacob"

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Jacob figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [all those descended from Jacob]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 9:9 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֤ה

"behold"

Amos is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [surely you will see that]

See: Foreground Information

title: Amos 9:9 (#2)
content:
אָֽנֹכִי֙ מְצַוֶּ֔ה

"I am commanding"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I am commanding that this happen]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 9:9 (#3)
content:
וַ⁠הֲנִע֥וֹתִי בְ⁠כָֽל־הַ⁠גּוֹיִ֖ם אֶת־בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר יִנּ֨וֹעַ֙ בַּ⁠כְּבָרָ֔ה

"and I will shake the house of Israel among all of the nations, just as it is shaken in the sieve"

The point of this comparison is that just as grain is shaken in the sieve in order to sort it, so Yahweh will shake the house of Israel among all of the nations, which included exile and dispersement among other nations, in order to separate the faithful people from the unfaithful ones. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I will shake the house of Israel among all of the nations to separate the faithful from the unfaithful, just as grain is shaken in a sieve to separate it from stones]

See: Simile

title: Amos 9:9 (#4)
content:
אֶת־בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל

"the house of Israel"

Yahweh is speaking of all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel, as if they were one house. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 9:9 (#5)
content:
כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר יִנּ֨וֹעַ֙ בַּ⁠כְּבָרָ֔ה

"just as it is shaken in the sieve"

The expression is shaken is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [just as someone shakes grain in a sieve]

See: Active or Passive

title: Amos 9:9 (#6)
content:
בַּ⁠כְּבָרָ֔ה

"in the sieve"

A sieve is a kind of container with holes in the bottom that a farmer shakes in order to separate grain from stones and dirt. If your readers would not be familiar with what a sieve is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in a screen for sifting grain]

See: Translate Unknowns

title: Amos 9:9 (#7)
content:
וְ⁠לֹֽא־יִפּ֥וֹל צְר֖וֹר אָֽרֶץ

"and a pebble will not fall to the earth"

The meaning of the word translated as pebble could also be translated as “small grain,” and thus it is uncertain whether the grain stays in the sieve or passes through. In either case, the meaning of the comparison is the same; God is using the nations as a sieve to sort out the people of Israel into those who are faithful to him (the grain) and those who are not (the stones). You may want to choose how you translate this comparison depending on whether the grain in your area is bigger or smaller than the holes in a sieve. To summarize, this word could mean: (1) a small stone. In this case, the sieve is retaining the stones and letting the grain fall through, as in the ULT and UST. (2) a small piece of something, such as grain. In this case, the sieve is retaining the grain and letting the small stones fall through. Alternate translation: [and a small grain will not fall to the earth]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 9:10 (#1)
content:
הָ⁠אֹמְרִ֗ים לֹֽא־תַגִּ֧ישׁ וְ⁠תַקְדִּ֛ים בַּעֲדֵ֖י⁠נוּ הָ⁠רָעָֽה

"the ones saying, ‘The evil will not approach or reach as far as us"

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [the ones saying that the evil will not approach or reach as far as them]

See: Quotes within Quotes

title: Amos 9:10 (#2)
content:
לֹֽא־תַגִּ֧ישׁ וְ⁠תַקְדִּ֛ים בַּעֲדֵ֖י⁠נוּ הָ⁠רָעָֽה

"The evil will not approach or reach as far as us"

The sinners are speaking of suffering harm as if The evil were a living thing that could approach or reach them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We will not suffer any harm]

See: Personification

title: Amos 9:10 (#3)
content:
הָ⁠רָעָֽה

"The evil"

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of evil, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Bad things]

See: Abstract Nouns

title: Amos 9:11 (#1)
content:
בַּ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠ה֔וּא

"In that day"

Yahweh is using the phrase translated as In that day to introduce a time of restoration. Unlike this phrase elsewhere in the book, it does not seem to indicate the time of punishment as in the “day of Yahweh” but the restoration that can occur because it is now possible.

See: Introduction of a New Event

title: Amos 9:11 (#2)
content:
אָקִ֛ים אֶת־סֻכַּ֥ת דָּוִ֖יד הַ⁠נֹּפֶ֑לֶת

"I will raise up the fallen booth of David"

Yahweh is speaking as if the dynasty or kingdom of David were a booth, a temporary shelter, that had collapsed and that he would restore or raise up again. He goes on to speak of repairing its breaches and rebuilding its ruins. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will restore the fallen dynasty of David]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 9:11 (#3)
content:
אֶת־פִּרְצֵי⁠הֶ֗ן

"their breaches"

The pronoun their probably refers to the cities of David’s kingdom. It may be clearer to use a singular pronoun to refer to the kingdom itself. Alternate translation: [its breaches]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

title: Amos 9:12 (#1)
content:
אֲשֶׁר־נִקְרָ֥א שְׁמִ֖⁠י עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֑ם

"whom my name is called over them"

Yahweh is using my name is called over them as a common expression of the culture to mean “they belong to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that belong to me]

See: Idiom

title: Amos 9:12 (#2)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֖ה עֹ֥שֶׂה זֹּֽאת

"the declaration of Yahweh, the one doing this"

Amos, who is conveying Yahweh’s words, is once again interjecting the declaration of Yahweh and this time adding the one doing this to emphasize that what has been said will surely happen as it is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 9:13 (#1)
content:
הִנֵּ֨ה יָמִ֤ים בָּאִים֙

"Behold, days are coming"

Yahweh is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say about the days or the specific time that is coming. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention, for the time is coming]

See: Foreground Information

title: Amos 9:13 (#2)
content:
נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה

"the declaration of Yahweh"

Amos, who is conveying Yahweh’s words, is once again interjecting the declaration of Yahweh to emphasize that what is about to be said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

See: Quotations and Quote Margins

title: Amos 9:13 (#3)
content:
וְ⁠נִגַּ֤שׁ חוֹרֵשׁ֙ בַּ⁠קֹּצֵ֔ר וְ⁠דֹרֵ֥ךְ עֲנָבִ֖ים בְּ⁠מֹשֵׁ֣ךְ הַ⁠זָּ֑רַע

"and the plower will approach the reaper, and the treader of grapes to the sower of the seed"

The implication is that the harvests will be so large that the plowing and planting seasons will begin before the reaping and the treading of grapes are finished. This was one of the covenant promises mentioned in Leviticus 26:5. You could include this information in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

title: Amos 9:13 (#4)
content:
וְ⁠דֹרֵ֥ךְ עֲנָבִ֖ים בְּ⁠מֹשֵׁ֣ךְ הַ⁠זָּ֑רַע

"and the treader of grapes to the sower of the seed"

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the treader of grapes will approach the sower of the seed]

See: Ellipsis

title: Amos 9:13 (#5)
content:
וְ⁠הִטִּ֤יפוּ הֶֽ⁠הָרִים֙ עָסִ֔יס וְ⁠כָל־הַ⁠גְּבָע֖וֹת תִּתְמוֹגַֽגְנָה

"and the mountains will drip sweet wine, and all of the hills will melt"

Yahweh is speaking as if the mountains and the hills themselves were producing sweet wine in such quantity that it flowed down their slopes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the vineyards on the mountains and the hills will produce great amounts of sweet wine]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 9:14 (#1)
content:
וְ⁠שַׁבְתִּי֮ אֶת־שְׁב֣וּת

"And I will restore the restoration of"

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. This could mean: (1) that he will restore the prosperity of his people as it was before they were exiled, as in the UST, or (2) that he will bring his exiled people back to their land. Alternate translation: [And I will restore from their exile]

See: Poetry

title: Amos 9:15 (#1)
content:
וּ⁠נְטַעְתִּ֖י⁠ם עַל־אַדְמָתָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠לֹ֨א יִנָּתְשׁ֜וּ ע֗וֹד מֵ⁠עַ֤ל אַדְמָתָ⁠ם֙

"And I will plant them upon their ground, and they will not be uprooted again from upon their ground"

Yahweh is speaking of restoring the Israelites to their land as if they were plants that he would plant in the ground that would never be uprooted again. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will settle them permanently in their land, and they will not be driven out again from upon the land]

See: Metaphor

title: Amos 9:15 (#2)
content:
וְ⁠לֹ֨א יִנָּתְשׁ֜וּ ע֗וֹד מֵ⁠עַ֤ל אַדְמָתָ⁠ם֙

"and they will not be uprooted again from upon their ground"

The expression be uprooted is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one will uproot them again from upon their ground]

See: Active or Passive

title: Amos 9:15 (#3)
content:
אֱלֹהֶֽי⁠ךָ

"your God"

Amos is not using this possessive form your God to indicate that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather, he is using these words to remind them that Yahweh is the God who chose them and whom they should worship. Alternate translation: [the God whom you worship]

See: Possession
